schools.summary: Keil and Delitzsch make this the one important event recorded from the thirty-seven years, with time and place unrecorded; Ellicott argues for Kadesh and traces both grievances — Korah passed over in the priestly family, the Reubenites stripped of the birthright and the leadership.

Gill sets out the cousinship of Korah with Moses and Aaron through Kohath; Calvin refuses to treat the two hundred and fifty as followers, since each expected a prize, and calls ambition never destitute of a specious excuse.
Henry turns the shared camp-side into the proverb about a wicked man's neighbour, and leaves the silence about On unexplained.

Wesley traces the malcontent to Elizaphan of the fourth son of Kohath being preferred over the line of the second; Clarke argues from the singular verb and the missing word "men" that Korah alone took the others.

debates.question: What does the opening verb govern?
positions: Clarke and Calvin: Korah alone acted, taking Dathan and Abiram with him
the received version supplies "men" as the object

debates.question: Where and when did the rebellion happen?
positions: Keil and Delitzsch: unrecorded, with no firm ground for conjecture
Ellicott: probably at Kadesh, during the blank between the two encampments

themes: Korah the ringleader, cousin to Moses and Aaron
the Reubenite grievance over the lost birthright
two hundred and fifty princes, each expecting a prize

schools.summary: Ellicott allows both "you have held it long enough" and "let it be enough to be of a holy people", and judges that Korah claimed a universal priesthood with the chief place in it for himself; Keil and Delitzsch note that both words for the congregation stand in the same verse.
Calvin hears a charge of sacrilege — that Moses and Aaron had robbed God of his supreme authority — and answers that holiness neither destroys subordination nor releases believers from obedience.
Clarke paraphrases the two Hebrew words as a complaint that holy offices are not equally distributed; Wesley splits the accusation between Moses prescribing the law and Aaron usurping the office.

themes: ye take too much upon you
all the congregation are holy
holiness does not abolish subordination

4.pericope_label: Moses falls on his face, and the trial by incense

schools.summary: Keil and Delitzsch read the prostration as a complaint carried to the Lord and explain why incense was chosen — the holiest priestly function, upon which God had already sanctified himself in judgment; Ellicott dates the trial to the morning and lets the delay save On and the sons of Korah.

Calvin contrasts the obstinacy that stands for virtue in unbelievers with the supplication of a man who knows all events are in God's hand, and reads the postponement as time granted for repentance; Gill has Moses speak only once the answer came.

Wesley makes the petition a request for direction and vindication and morning the hour of judgment among men; Clarke hears the phrase again in Paul and reads the retort of v. 7 as a verdict on their fitness for any spiritual employment.

outliers: Clarke derives the seal of 2 Timothy 2:19 from this verse, and reads the accompanying exhortation as an allusion to v. 26.
themes: even to morrow the LORD will shew who are his
the trial by censers
a night granted for repentance

8.pericope_label: seemeth it but a small thing

schools.summary: Ellicott follows the Targums in making the office Korah wanted the high priesthood itself, above what the rest of his company sought.

Calvin explains why a speech to the tribe is addressed to Korah alone, and finds the sin in ingratitude — the more liberally a man has been dealt with, the more intolerable his aspiring higher; Gill details what nearness to God meant in practice for a Levite.
Henry counts the three privileges of the Levites and argues that undervaluing an allowed honour is what makes a man grasp at a forbidden one.
Wesley calls the office a high dignity, though not sufficient for ambitious minds.

outliers: Calvin turns the phrase against the Pope, demanding that anyone who likens his opponents to Korah first produce the credentials of his own calling.
themes: the Levites already brought near
ye are gathered together against the LORD
what is Aaron, that ye murmur against him?

12.pericope_label: Dathan and Abiram refuse the summons

schools.summary: Ellicott marks the perverse transfer of the promise to Egypt and notes that the phrase about the eyes is used literally of Samson.

Calvin sees Egypt deliberately unnamed while its fruitfulness is magnified, so that God's blessing might be buried, and reads Moses' anger as free of reviling — he asks only that the offering be refused; Gill renders the anger as heat, kindled by the dishonour done to God.
Henry takes the four charges in order and answers each from the history, ending with the ass never taken and the wages never drawn.
Wesley explains the idiom of going up to judgment; Clarke says there was no danger of the offering being accepted, God blessing no scheme of salvation of man's appointment.

themes: we will not come up
a land flowing with milk and honey, said of Egypt
I have not taken one ass from them

16.pericope_label: the censers brought, and the congregation gathered

schools.summary: Ellicott offers three accounts of where the censers came from and finds in the wording a general disposition in the people to favour the insurrection.

Calvin denies that the summons was an experiment, Moses being assured by the Spirit of prophecy, and reads the gathered crowd as an ostentatious hardening — smoke interposed against the sun; Gill passes on Jarchi's account of Korah canvassing the tribes by night.
Henry sets the appearing glory beside the one that installed Aaron, and calls it the most terrible of sights to men conscious of guilt.
Wesley explains why the trial was held at the door rather than within, and traces the fire to the altar because of what strange fire had cost Nadab and Abihu.

themes: two hundred and fifty censers at the door
Korah gathers the congregation
the glory of the LORD appeared

20.pericope_label: separate yourselves — and the prayer that answers

schools.summary: Keil and Delitzsch treat assembling before the tabernacle as making common cause with the rebels; Ellicott says the congregation had by that obedience become partakers in Korah's sin.

Calvin compares the command with the drawing of Lot out of Sodom, distinguishes a sentence of desert from a secret decree, and denies that God takes on new feelings when he is said to be moved by prayer; Gill notes that the order names the whole congregation and not merely the two hundred and fifty.
Henry hears Abraham at Sodom in the closing question, and grants that the great transgression belonged to the man who first hatched the treason.
Clarke takes the title as proof that these men held soul and body to be distinct principles; Wesley unfolds it into four pleas — maker, preserver, father and searcher of spirits.

debates.question: What does "the spirits of all flesh" establish?
positions: Clarke: that man is compounded of flesh and an immortal spirit, the word not meaning breath here
Calvin: that each man has his own spirit created, against the Manichean single spirit

themes: the God of the spirits of all flesh
shall one man sin, and wilt thou be wroth with all?
a sentence pronounced and a prayer heard

23.pericope_label: depart from the tents of these wicked men

schools.summary: Ellicott weighs whether the word means a rival tabernacle or, collectively, the tents of the three, and prefers the latter because the command as delivered says tents; he also notes what the verse omits — Korah's position, and the sons who did not die.

Calvin defends the harshness of calling them wicked men as an urgent exhortation rather than anger, takes the obedience of the people as evidence that most had been carried away by levity, and says the two stood like maniacs.
Henry has Dathan and Abiram keeping court in a rival tent, and draws from the warning that no one may reap the benefit of a friend's prayers who will not use the means of salvation himself.
Wesley adds that the elders went for the greater solemnity of the act.

themes: get you up from about the tabernacle of Korah
touch nothing of theirs
they stood in the door of their tents

28.pericope_label: if the LORD make a new thing

schools.summary: Ellicott renders the wager literally — create a creation — and glosses the pit as Sheol.

Calvin explains that the contest was pressed this far so that God might sanction his own institution publicly, and hears the memory of the judgment in the psalm that prays for the wicked to go down alive; Gill lists what Moses was on trial for and takes the common death to be fever or old age.
Henry argues that a judgment foretold with no natural indication proved more about the man who foretold it than the judgment alone could.

Wesley separates natural death from the usual judgments and puts Moses' offer in the plainest terms; Clarke argues from the households and children swallowed that the word must mean a chasm and not the place of the lost.

themes: I have not done them of mine own mind
create a creation
they go down quick into the pit

fidelity.note: The clause explaining why fire from heaven was named among the ordinary deaths joins two of Henry's statements — his list of precedented judgments and his calling the earthquake "a punishment without precedent" — into an inference he does not state in that form.

31.pericope_label: the earth opens, and the fire falls

schools.summary: Keil and Delitzsch read the households as families rather than tents; Ellicott builds the case that Korah died by fire with his company, from the sons who lived, from Deuteronomy and from the psalm that divides the two punishments.

Calvin thinks the diversity of punishment deliberate, each receiving according to the measure of his iniquity, and reads the people's flight as the mark of a bad conscience; Gill lets the earth open its mouth as a beast of prey and supplies the Targum on what the dying cried.
Henry keeps in view that Aaron stood among the men the fire consumed and was preserved.
Wesley argues from command that a captain would not desert his men, and supposes the sons absent on service; Clarke sums the judgment as two punishments for the rebels' two divisions.

debates.question: Did Korah go down into the chasm or die in the fire?
positions: Ellicott and Wesley: he stood with his company at the tabernacle door and was burned
the verse read alone, and the later summary that names him with Dathan and Abiram, suggest the chasm

themes: the ground clave asunder
they perished from among the congregation
fire from the LORD consumed the two hundred and fifty

36.pericope_label: the censers beaten into a covering for the altar

schools.summary: Keil and Delitzsch explain how the censers became holy and so fell to the Lord as banned things once their bearers were killed; Ellicott says Aaron was spared the work because he was about to be needed for intercession, and defends brass against the supposition of silver.

Calvin holds that they were preserved as accursed rather than as consecrated, the fire being flung away while the metal was kept, and that memory of judgment fails from neglect rather than ignorance; Gill takes the priests' own censers to have been silver.
Henry notes that they were not kept as censers, which would have honoured the usurpers, but laid over the altar they had challenged.
Wesley locates the unclean place where the coals were cast and describes bodies left where they fell; Clarke glosses the word as consecrated, improperly employed.

debates.question: In what sense were the censers hallowed?
positions: Calvin: set apart as accursed, under a ban
others: once devoted to holy use, and so not to be returned to common service

debates.question: What metal were the priests' own censers?
positions: Gill: silver, gold only on the day of atonement
Ellicott: brass, there being no sufficient authority for silver

themes: censers of sinners against their own souls
a covering for the altar
that no stranger come near to offer incense

41.pericope_label: the congregation murmurs, and the glory appears again

schools.summary: Keil and Delitzsch describe a covering fuller than the daily cloud, with the glory breaking out of it, and mark that this time the prayer did not avert the judgment; Ellicott suspects the cloud had been withdrawn the day before and was now restored.

Calvin asks whether Moses could command the earth or call down fire, counts the two absurdities of the charge, and reads the shelter of the cloud as a measure of how uncontrollable the rage had become; Gill takes the gathering for an attempt on their lives.
Henry says the charge canonises the rebels and, by accusing the two of murder, accuses God; and concludes that grace must do what terror could not.
Clarke suggests the people had persuaded themselves the earthquake and fire were contrived; Wesley sums the response as rendering good for evil.

outliers: Clarke alone offers a motive for the accusation — that the people took the earthquake and the fire for human contrivance.
themes: ye have killed the people of the LORD
the cloud covered it, and the glory appeared
get you up from among this congregation

46.pericope_label: Aaron stands between the dead and the living

schools.summary: Ellicott would read the censer as the high priest's golden one, and points to the offering of a sweet-smelling savour that Aaron here prefigures.

Calvin denies that the expiation depended on the incense and makes the censer a symbol to rouse repentance and point to an absent Saviour; he closes the argument the murmurers began, three hundred mourned and fifty times as many lost.
Henry describes Aaron's running as courage and charity together, and sets his censer against the censers of the sinners.
Wesley makes incense a sign of intercession which must be accompanied by it; Clarke explains the secret blast, and reasons from the priest with a censer to the atonement he prefigured.

themes: make an atonement for them: the plague is begun
he stood between the dead and the living
fourteen thousand and seven hundred
